entries.title: U.S. moves long-range bombers from U.K. And, Israel allegedly warned before Oct. 7
entries.summary: A possible Iranian threat led the U.S. to remove long-range bombers from a U.K. base. And, Israelis are learning that their prime minister may have been warned before the Oct. 7 attacks.
entries.content:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

New information reveals that, over the weekend, the U.S. removed all long-range bombers from the British air base near where five men were arrested last week in a suspected terror plot. A U.S. official who is not authorized to speak publicly told NPR that the decision to abruptly send home a dozen B-1 bombers from Royal Air Force base Fairford was due to a "credible threat" from Iran, which potentially involved a drone attack.

  • 🎧 The war with Iran has shown that U.S. military bases, both at home and abroad, are now seen as more vulnerable, NPR's Greg Myre tells Up First. Iranian drones and missiles have targeted U.S. bases across the Middle East since the start of the conflict. For the past three decades, the U.S. has established these bases to protect its allies, but the rise of drone threats has changed this perspective. Now, the U.S. must defend a network of military bases — a task that is complicated and costly, Myre says.

High school students in France are blocking schools today, after hundreds of thousands of them marched across the country yesterday. They are joined by teachers, parents and labor union members. The movement, which began in a particularly run-down high school facing teacher absenteeism, aims to improve learning conditions and address inequalities in the French education system.

  • 🎧 The French school system plays a crucial role in shaping the national identity, promoting the idea that anyone can achieve their goals if they apply themselves in l'école de la Republique, or the school of the republic, NPR's Eleanor Beardsley says. She adds that this concept is at the heart of France's democracy and vision of itself as a meritocracy and egalitarian society. Even elite public schools in Paris are joining the movement. French news reports show clashes between youth and police and cars, trash cans and schools burning. Initially, the far-right condemned delinquency, but many also saw police aggression. Critics argue that the government responded too late and then framed the issue as urban violence instead of addressing the students' demands.

A former head of Germany's foreign intelligence agency will appear before a federal judge today to face charges of espionage and attempted treason. Federal prosecutors accuse August Hanning of using classified information to brief a foreign intelligence agency. He served as the head of Germany's CIA equivalent for seven years from 1998 to 2005. Prosecutors allege he shared sensitive political information for 12 years after leaving office. They have not yet disclosed who Hanning's alleged clients were.

  • 🎧 NPR's Esme Nicholson says that categorizing Hanning's alleged actions as a major setback to Germany's security apparatus is putting it mildly. Prosecutors allege that a former aide to Hanning leaked documents intended for high-level briefings, raising concerns among Germany's western allies about the credibility of its intelligence agencies and whether their own agents have been compromised. This arrest coincides with a warning from Martin Jaeger, Germany's new foreign intelligence chief, that Russia is waging a "shadow war" in Germany through sabotage, cyber attacks, and disinformation campaigns. Nicholson says the consequences of this conflict are not only humiliating but also potentially dangerous.

As Israel marks three years since Hamas' surprise Oct. 7 attacks, new reports in Israeli and U.S. media say regional allies warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Hamas was planning to attack. Four people in the Middle East with direct knowledge of the warnings told NPR that Netanyahu was personally informed about the potential attacks and his security agencies were notified multiple times in the weeks and days leading up to Oct. 7, 2023. Netanyahu has denied this, labeling the reports "fake news" and recently filing a defamation lawsuit against the news outlets that first published the information. He and his defense minister now warn that Hamas might attempt to attack again on this Oct. 7 memorial day and leading up to Israel's national elections later this month.

Living better

Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.

Parental monitoring plays a key role in shielding kids from the dangers of social media and excessive screen time. Parents can empower their children to navigate the digital world confidently and safely by establishing clear boundaries early and having open conversations about online habits. Here are some ways guardians can help their kids use their devices more safely:

  • 📱 Put the phone away during meals and bedtime. This will help protect sleep and reduce the risk of eating disorders.
  • 📱 Apply rules around screen time to the whole family, including parents and guardians.
  • 📱 Ask children open-minded questions about what they are doing online. Open communication helps kids feel comfortable sharing what they experience online.
  • 📱 Establish early communication with children about cyberbullying, online scams, Instagram filters and privacy issues for their awareness.

On the ground

The results of the 2026 midterm elections will shape the final two years of President Trump's second term and serve as a precursor to the 2028 general election. This month, Morning Edition is reporting from six states that could change the balance of power in Washington.

Morning Edition's Leila Fadel traveled to the battleground state of Maine to discover what issues are energizing voters. Maine residents could play a crucial role in deciding which political party controls the Senate. One of the most significant U.S. Senate races features Republican incumbent Susan Collins, who is seeking re-election against Democrat Troy Jackson. The race has been closely watched, especially after Jackson was nominated by the Maine Democratic Party after Graham Platner withdrew because of a sexual assault allegation. Listen to what has been happening in that contest.

Fadel was also on the ground with residents, figuring out what they cared about. Hear more about:

  • 🎧 How the Trump administration's immigration enforcement has divided residents.
  • 🎧 Whether Democratic policies and candidates are resonating, and why so many men voted for Trump in 2024.
  • 🎧 How the economy and other key issues are influencing voters' decisions in the midterm elections.

Follow the reporting: Texas coverage airs Oct. 13, followed by reporting from North Carolina and Georgia, and Ohio and Michigan. You can follow along on Morning Edition, NPR.org, in the NPR app and in the Up First newsletter.

3 things to know before you go

  • The 2026 National Book Awards finalists are here, showcasing a diverse range of literary works, from nonfiction on the prison system to a novel about a patient navigator at a gender-affirming care center.
  • Avengers: Endgame has reclaimed the number one position on Hollywood's all-time worldwide box office chart following its recent re-release in cinemas. It first became the highest-grossing film in history in 2019.
  • Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have earned the 2026 Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine for their contributions to optogenetics, a field of neuroscience that examines the links between neuron activity and specific behaviors. Soon after learning of his win, Deisseroth spoke with Here & Now. (via WBUR)

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

entries.title: Who will win the 2026 Nobel Prize in economics?
entries.summary: A thinly traded prediction market offers a starting point. We explore potential winners and the big ideas that could earn them economics' biggest prize.
entries.content:
Who will win the 2026 Nobel Prize in economics?

And the winner of the 2026 Nobel Prize in economics is … we don't know yet. That announcement is scheduled for Monday, and we'll be covering it here in the Planet Money newsletter and The Indicator podcast.

In the meantime, the week before the announcement is a great time to partake in a nerdy pastime: remembering all the amazing economics research that hasn't yet gotten a Swedish medal, and guessing who might get the world's most coveted wake-up call.

One quick note: The official name is the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. It's a mouthful, so we'll stick with "Nobel Prize in economics." Unlike the original Nobel Prizes, this one wasn't established by Alfred Nobel's will. Sweden's central bank created it in 1968 — a history we'll explore in a forthcoming episode of The Indicator.

Many factors go into choosing a Nobel laureate. Winners tend to be older, partly because the committee wants the passage of time to help them assess the candidates' impact on the field and/or broader world. Sometimes the committee picks research that speaks to the zeitgeist. Other times it's because of very technical work that has given economists stronger empirical tools to study the world.

So how might we make a guess? Well, there's one tool that economists love for making predictions: markets. Markets can aggregate the scattered information held by countless people, boiling down what they know about the world into a single number: a price — an idea famously articulated by economist Friedrich von Hayek, who, naturally, won a Nobel Prize back in 1974.

Those prices can sometimes offer clues about the future. For example, take the stock market. Many economists view it as a kind of giant information-processing machine. In this view, a company's stock price reflects the crowd's beliefs about that company's future profits. It can provide a kind of crystal ball. Although, of course, the crowd can be wrong.

[🎧 There is, of course, a classic Planet Money episode about this, and also about a cow.]

The same idea applies to prediction markets, which have really taken off in recent years. Instead of betting on a company's future profits, traders bet on whether a particular event will happen — say, who will win a Nobel Prize.

And, wouldn't you know it, there's a prediction market for who will win the 2026 Nobel in economics. There's just one problem: It's incredibly small, or as traders might call it, thin. Maybe economists are too rational — or too busy — to bet on something this unpredictable?

As of this writing Tuesday afternoon, Oct. 6, this prediction market for who will win the 2026 prize had recorded about $11,000 in trading volume. For comparison, Kalshi's main market for the 2024 presidential election recorded about $670 million — tens of thousands of times as much. That prediction market correctly favored Donald Trump to win the election.

With such little trading, however, this Nobel prediction market seems less like the wisdom of crowds, and more like the guesstimates of a small number of nerdy gamblers. As we sat down to write this on Tuesday, Oct. 6, we watched, somewhat frustratingly, as the market swung wildly over who was favored to win based on what seemed to be relatively small new bets.

But let's give this prediction market the benefit of the doubt and call it a starting point. It at least provides an excuse to explore some big economic ideas and methods and the people behind them.

By late Tuesday afternoon, we decided to stop hitting refresh. Ariel Pakes and Susan Athey were trading places at the top of Kalshi's rankings, with Robert Barro rounding out the top three.

Ariel Pakes: What happens when competitors merge?

Ariel Pakes is an economist at Harvard University who has made big contributions to an area of economics known as industrial organization. It studies how industries are organized and how that structure affects competition and the prices and choices of consumers. For example, how do prices and product offerings differ when a market is dominated by a single company versus many competing ones?

In 1995, Pakes, together with Steven Berry and James Levinsohn, published a landmark paper about the American automobile industry. The method they developed, known as BLP, helps economists figure out how consumers choose among competing products. Those estimates can help simulate whether a proposed merger or acquisition will raise prices, and by how much.

This isn't just an academic exercise. The BLP model has evolved over time, and antitrust regulators use these tools to estimate how a proposed merger could affect consumers — giving them evidence to weigh when deciding whether to challenge a deal.

Why has Pakes been leading the pack on Kalshi? Maybe it's because antitrust is hot right now, and his research speaks to the zeitgeist. Maybe it's because the empirical tools he's helped develop have had a considerable impact on policymaking. Or maybe it's because one high roller placed a bet with inside knowledge, or because they were like a Pakes superfan … We can't know. Anyways, moving on.

Susan Athey: Using machine learning to understand cause and effect

Susan Athey is the economics of technology professor at Stanford Graduate School of Business. As her title hints, she is a leading authority on the economics of digital technology, from the internet to cryptocurrencies to artificial intelligence.

Athey has been a prolific scholar. In 2007, she won the John Bates Clark Medal, a top prize for economists under 40 who make "the most significant contribution to economic thought and knowledge." The American Economic Association cited her contributions to "economic theory, empirical economics, and econometrics." She was the first woman to win the prize.

Since then, Athey has continued to tackle a wide range of topics. We previously cited her theoretical work aimed at designing a market that creates incentives to remove carbon from the atmosphere and slow or reverse climate change.

Athey also helped pioneer the use of machine learning — a branch of artificial intelligence — in economics. Machine learning is good at finding patterns in data and making predictions. Athey and her collaborators have helped adapt those tools to answer questions about cause and effect. For example, does a job-training program help workers make more money, and which workers see bigger benefits?

In addition to her theoretical and empirical contributions to the field, Athey has been an outspoken critic of her field's culture of bullying, discrimination, and sexual harassment. We spoke to her back in 2019, when the profession was reckoning with the underrepresentation and mistreatment of women amid the MeToo movement.

Robert Barro: Why expectations matter

Next up: Robert Barro. He's another economist at Harvard University. He, alongside Nobel laureates like Robert Lucas and Thomas Sargent, helped reshape modern macroeconomics around a simple idea: people and businesses look ahead, and policymakers have to account for that. Their expectations about future taxes, inflation, and government actions shape how they respond to efforts to stimulate the economy or control inflation.

Barro is particularly known for helping to develop a theory known as "Ricardian equivalence." The basic gist: if the government cuts people's taxes by borrowing, that may have a smaller stimulative effect than policymakers hope. That's because people anticipate that the resulting debt will eventually require higher taxes — and they may decide to save the extra money instead of spending it. Ricardian is a reference to the 19th century British economist David Ricardo. "Equivalence" refers to the idea that, under certain assumptions, taxing people now or borrowing and taxing them later has the same effect on consumer spending. That's because, according to this theory, people will save the extra money to cover higher taxes down the road.

This idea has been hotly debated for decades. Critics stress that many households don't plan that far ahead, and those who are short on cash tend to spend the money instead of saving it.

Other potential winners

As we stated above, not many people seem to be betting at the Kalshi prediction market on the 2026 Nobel Prize in economics. And their rankings hardly exhaust the possibilities. Here are some other potential contenders:

Thomas Piketty and Emmanuel Saez: Tracking the rise of the very rich. Piketty is a professor of Economics at the Paris School of Economics. Saez is at UC Berkeley. The two did pathbreaking work on inequality that helped get us talking about "the one percent." (Check out our recent episode of Planet Money, "Middlegarchs are the new oligarchs," which touches on this research.)

Raj Chetty: Mapping the American Dream. If you read this newsletter, you probably know we're fanboys and fangirls of Raj. He's an economist at Harvard University, and he and his many collaborators have used massive government datasets and clever empirical methods to tackle some of the biggest questions in economics, including a bunch of work on how to revitalize the American Dream. (Raj Chetty has been a fixture in the Planet Money newsletter and podcast; check out: "Why the American Dream is more attainable in some cities than others"; "This housing program helped kids escape poverty — by changing who they befriended"; and "Affirmative action for rich kids: It's more than just legacy admissions.")

David Autor: How technology and trade reshape work. Autor, of MIT, is one of the most influential labor economists of our time. His research has helped transform our understanding of how technology changes work. He and his collaborators helped explain how the computer revolution contributed to growing income inequality. He also, of course, did very influential research on the "China Shock," which is still shaping heated conversations about the effects of free trade on the economy. (We've explored Autor's work many times in the Planet Money newsletter and podcasts. For a taste, check out "What if AI could rebuild the middle class?"; "Why economists got free trade with China so wrong"; "Are Cities Overrated?"; and "What the future of work means for cities.")

Janet Currie: Showing how childhood matters for the economy. Currie, an economist at Yale, has done a bunch of important work on how the conditions kids grow up in shape their economic outcomes as adults. Her research explores how disadvantages, from poverty to pollution, can have lasting consequences. And she's studied how various government programs can improve kids' health and ultimately their economic prospects.

Of course, some of these are our picks, and they're not listed on Kalshi. And newsletter writers, no matter how well-versed in the economics literature, don't have crystal balls. Nor do prediction markets. They merely aggregate information from a crowd of people willing to bet about the future. And, in the case of this prediction market, that crowd doesn't seem very big.

Stay tuned for next week's Planet Money newsletter for our analysis of who ended up actually winning the prize and why. If you're not already subscribed, you can subscribe here: npr.org/planetmoneynewsletter.

entries.title: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai win Nobel Prize in chemistry
entries.summary: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry Wednesday for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.
entries.content:
Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai win Nobel Prize in chemistry

STOCKHOLM — Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry Wednesday for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.

"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously," Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said in a news release. "The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."

The duo's discoveries, the news release said, "have been decisive for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals."

Kagan, born in France, is affiliated with Université Paris-Sud in Orsay, France, and Soai, 95 years old and born in Japan, with the Tokyo University of Science.

The so-called "Soai reaction" is named for the scientist's experiment.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winner in Stockholm.

Last year, three scientists won the chemistry Nobel for their development of new molecular structures that can trap vast quantities of gas inside, laying the groundwork to potentially suck greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere or harvest moisture from desert environments.

This year's prizes began with the Nobel for medicine, awarded Monday to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award Tuesday recognized a scientist's efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos.

The literature prize is set to be awarded Thursday. After Friday's peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates or an organization.

entries.title: Here's the latest sticker shock: Borrowing for a mortgage -- or a car
entries.summary: It's not just mortgages being at their highest level in almost three years — but the cost of loans for cars and higher education are among the borrowing costs affected, too.
entries.content:
Here's the latest sticker shock: Borrowing for a mortgage — or a car

Carrie Goldstein's dream for a new home started with a family reunion at her cousin's home in Milwaukee. The home was old with character and she could walk anywhere from the front door.

"We were kind of in awe and drooling over her walkability," Goldstein says.

It was the lifestyle Goldstein wanted but lacked in her Cleveland suburb, which she says is also pretty walkable – with one major issue.

"There are lots of sidewalks," she says. "But you can't really go anywhere."

She brainstormed with her husband and realized nearby Rocky River was where they wanted to live. It was still a suburb, but with a quaint downtown and the option to walk to Lake Erie.

But as much as she wanted to move, one thing stopped her cold. The mortgage she would have to pay. Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home impossible for many people at a time when housing prices are also sky high.

Goldstein is running into a problem that's affecting many households at a time when people have already been struggling with years of high inflation: The rising cost of borrowing.

Bond markets influence all types of borrowing costs across the economy – and as yields have surged to their highest in decades, they've pushed up all kinds of interest rates paid by consumers, from loans for homes to cars and higher education.

And those rates are likely to continue moving up after the Federal Reserve in September raised interest rates for the first time this year – while signaling an additional hike could come this year.

Rate hikes from the Federal Reserve filter through the economy and are meant to slow down consumer and business spending by making people hesitant to take out a more expensive loan to pay for a car or a home – both essential purchases for many people.

"If you need to borrow, boy, it's really not a good time," says John Diamond, senior director of the Center for Tax and Budget Policy at the Baker Institute.

The housing market remains in the slumps

Buying a home is a key example of how households are affected when borrowing costs rise in the economy.

While mortgage rates were falling at the start of this year, they reversed upward after the U.S. war with Iran spooked the bond market by raising worries about inflation. As a result, mortgage rates, which are influenced by the bond markets, have surged this year.

For example, at the current 7.28% level for the average 30-year fixed rate mortgage, a person could end up paying about $900 more compared with the 3% pandemic-era rates for a median priced home.

As expected, fewer homeowners are willing or capable of making that financial leap, even if they have long since outgrown their current home. Existing house sales in August were down about 1.2% from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors.

Car loans are about to get more expensive

It's not just mortgage costs that are making Americans like Goldstein wince.

Alongside her dreams of owning a home in a walkable neighborhood, Goldstein is ready for a new car. Her old one is 11 years old, has 150,000 miles and plenty of quirks. The repair costs are approaching the point where they'll be more than the value of the actual car.

But a four-year loan for a used car is about three percentage points higher compared with the start of 2022, right around when auto loans began to shed their pandemic-era low rates and started climbing up.

"You can't go and get a car for $150 or $180 bucks anymore a month," she says about the car payments she would be facing.

Although so far the Fed has only delivered a modest quarter of a percentage point, it's adding to the higher borrowing costs at a time when households are already dealing with inflation and higher prices for other types of borrowing.

"It's added to higher mortgage payments. Higher student loan payments. Higher prices because of inflation," Diamond says. "That's what makes it really painful."

And that could mean that households could continue to delay any big purchases requiring a loan.

Goldstein is one of them. She says she can afford to wait on the car and house. But eventually she unsubscribed from real estate updates for that walkable suburb.

"It just became more and more disheartening when I did the math," Goldstein says. "It's just not in the cards."

entries.title: Over 1,000 children are buried at juvenile detention centers nationwide
entries.summary: Researchers uncovered the graves of more than 1,000 children next to juvenile detention facilities in 29 states. At one Maryland gravesite, 230 Black boys are buried.
entries.content:
Over 1,000 children are buried at juvenile detention centers nationwide

When Veronica Spears read the letter, she began to shake.

"What's wrong?" her husband asked.

At the time, she said, she couldn't find the words to respond.

"The letter said they found out that my grandfather had a brother that was in a reformation institution," she later told NPR in an interview. "And he passed away at the age of 12. We never knew."

Spears' family is one of 16 that researchers with Georgetown University's Center for Youth Justice have linked to children who died at the House of Reformation and Instruction for Colored Children in Cheltenham, Md. The center has been working since February to identify children who died at 40 reform schools and youth detention centers across the country, as well as any surviving family members, as part of its Forgotten Children Initiative.

To date, the researchers have identified the graves of over 1,000 children across 29 states. The largest burial site is located near the House of Reformation, now the Cheltenham Youth Detention Center. More than 230 Black boys were found buried in the woods across the street from the facility.

The small headstones are easy to miss, especially in the fall, when they seem to sink into the fallen leaves. A few pieces of trash from a nearby worksite mix with the leaves.

Chuck Copeland, Spears' cousin, hiked through tall trees and thorny brush one morning in late September. A pastor who lives about two hours away, he leaned in to read one of the headstones.

"He didn't count for nothing. He meant nothing to them," he said, grimacing. Then he read, "Thirteen years old from Baltimore, Mark Davis, 1885."

Established in 1870, the House of Reformation, where Mark Davis died, was the first juvenile detention facility for Black children in the American South, according to the Georgetown researchers. It was created to get Black youth out of adult prisons. Children as young as 5 years old were incarcerated for criminal offenses, as well as a number of non-criminal reasons, including being poor, homeless or orphaned, researchers found.

While there, the boys were forced to work without food and disciplined by white guards with a "brass-studded belt," according to a report from the Maryland Department of Juvenile Services. In the 1920s, the boys were leased to neighboring farms, with the institution taking most, if not all, of their pay. They were also forced to work in the reformatory's broom factory in conditions described by Baltimore City labor union investigators in 1926 as a "firetrap," according to the report.

The Georgetown researchers have not discovered why Spears' great-uncle, Arthur Hamilton, was incarcerated in the institution, and they have not found his remains at the burial ground. The family was told he died of tuberculosis in 1917.

Marc Schindler was a senior official at the Maryland Department of Juvenile Services when the state rediscovered the burial ground in 2024. When he went to work for Georgetown University, he continued researching similar sites across the country. His team has so far found graves tied to 40 institutions, from Salem, Ore., to Augusta, Maine.

Some of the graves are next to juvenile detention centers still in operation.

"I'm hopeful that in states around the country, people will step forward and we can see an appropriate response to what I think is unquestionably a national tragedy," Schindler said.

As states learn about these burial sites, some state lawmakers around the country have begun looking at options for restitution. In Florida, lawmakers established a $20 million fund for survivors who attended an infamous reform school that closed in 2011. In Arkansas, officials created a memorial to honor 21 Black boys who died in a fire at a correctional facility in 1959.

This year, Maryland lawmakers created a commission to research and identify all the children buried in Cheltenham. The commission, housed in the state attorney general's office, includes family members of the children, who will weigh in on the future of the site and how the state should make amends for how it treated the children at the reform institution.

"Understanding this history is tremendously important, but understanding how this history connects to our current practices is almost probably more important," state Senator Will Smith, who sponsored the bill creating the commission, told NPR.

Smith pointed to Maryland laws that result in hundreds of children being charged as adults every year. He said accounting for the state's past involves changing those kinds of laws. And this year, the state legislature took a step toward that goal. After more than a decade of pressure from advocacy groups, lawmakers passed Smith's bill removing some offenses, such as firearm possession, from the list of charges that automatically send young people to be tried in adult court. That change took effect this month.

Smith credits a trip the legislature's Black caucus took to the gravesite in Cheltenham with convincing lawmakers to support the change.

When Spears and Copeland visited the gravesite that day in September, they eventually reached a place where there were no more headstones. What's left are rows of gray cinder blocks — over 200, with no names or dates. Researchers believe Arthur Hamilton is buried somewhere in this part of the woods. Spears said she believes it, too.

"I don't have any proof, no," she said, placing her hand over her chest. "I felt it in my chest. I felt a heaviness. I knew then he was crying out to all of us — they all were — to let us know we're here and we were mistreated."

She pursed her lips and looked at the ground. After a while, Spears, Copeland and other family members gathered in a circle among the cinder blocks. They were all silent until Copeland, the pastor, began speaking. He lamented the history he was taught. The history he was not taught. The betrayal he feels.

"The first thing I learned in school to memorize was the Pledge of Allegiance," he said. Then he raised his hands, gesturing toward the graves around him. "Liberty and justice for all." He shook his head as his hands landed with a thud at his sides.

After another moment of silence, Copeland led the family in a prayer.

"Thank you for this opportunity to remember our uncle Arthur Hamilton," he said.

Copeland said he wants the children to know they aren't forgotten anymore.

entries.title: An early flu season means it might be time to think about a flu shot
entries.summary: Flu season typically starts in October or November. But it looks like the flu started to pick up in September this year.
entries.content:
An early flu season means it might be time to think about a flu shot

An early start to flu season moves up vaccination timing

For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

Fall has only just begun, but it's already time to start thinking about the quintessential winter bug: the flu.

The annual flu season usually starts in October or November. But this year, it looks like the flu started to pick up in early September.

"There are enough signs pointing in the same direction to make me think, 'OK, yes. This is the start of flu season,'" says Caitlin Rivers, an epidemiologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

The percentage of people testing positive for the flu in the West has been rising steadily since around the beginning of September, she says. And the number of people showing up in emergency departments because of the flu has also been rising for weeks, she adds.

"It's very uncommon to see flu activity rising this early. It's activity that we might normally see more like November or December," she says.

The timing of the flu season isn't the only thing that's odd. It's also unusual that flu activity seems to have started in Western states, such as California, Washington, Hawaii and Alaska.

"It typically starts in the South and then expands from there," Rivers says. "So two uncommon developments there."

Rivers stresses that the amount of flu activity is still very low in most parts of the country. But that's starting to change as the flu picks up nationwide.

It's unclear why flu activity would have started so early, and in such an unusual part of the country. But one clue might be a new variant that evolved a mutation, which appears to make it better at evading existing immunity, especially among teenagers.

"That's our best argument for what's going on right now in terms of this early flu season," says Dr. Alex Greninger, a virologist who heads infectious disease diagnostics at the University of Washington. Doctors there are seeing as much flu right now as they usually would around Christmas, and the mutated variant appears to be common, he says.

So Greninger, Rivers and others are urging people to think about getting their flu shot earlier than usual.

"It's crucial that people get an influenza vaccine," says Scott Hensley, a virologist at the University of Pennsylvania. "And this might be a year that people might want to get a vaccine early."

But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention hasn't been promoting flu shots as it usually does. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who oversees the CDC, is a long-time vaccine skeptic.

"It is disappointing that CDC is quiet given that flu kills of hundreds of kids a year and can result in tens of thousands of hospitalizations and tens of thousands of deaths," says Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, who resigned last year as the director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to protest what he called political interference at the agency.

The CDC declined to make an official available to NPR for this story. In a statement, a CDC spokesperson said, "CDC is developing a communications strategy to provide clear, accessible information about influenza vaccination and other critical steps people can take to protect themselves during respiratory virus season. This includes information about the benefits and risks of vaccination to support informed decision-making."

entries.title: 'Medicare for All' message attracts midterm voters buckling under medical bills
entries.summary: Midterm candidates are talking up Medicare for All, and in a poll 2 out of 3 Americans said they support it. The phrase speaks to a desire for radical change, though many don't really know what it is.
entries.content:
Christina Starks-Clay doesn't know how "Medicare for All" would work exactly, but she's willing to bet it'd be better than what she has now.

While standing in line for a Sept. 11 town hall for U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Lansing, she whipped out her phone and pulled up a screenshot.

It was of the $1,000 cashier's check she'd picked up at the bank that day to pay down a chunk of her son's dental bills.

Starks-Clay, an early childhood special education paraprofessional, still owed the dentist $389, even with good dental insurance. Her own cleaning a few weeks before had cost $600.

She tried to talk herself down at the bank, to focus on being grateful for what she could afford.

"I'm like, 'Tina, OK, you were in a position for this moment to do this,'" she said. "A lot of people couldn't do what I had to do today. I couldn't do it. But I did it. So I need to hear, how are you going to make this better for everyone?"

Many who waited in the hot sun that afternoon in a line stretching blocks through downtown Lansing shared similar anxieties.

A man ahead of Starks-Clay talked about watching his brother rack up thousands of dollars in medical debt.

A professor emeritus at nearby Michigan State University worried aloud about his grandkids' medical care, because his adult kids were struggling to meet a $9,000 insurance deductible.

Healthcare workers who'd turned up for the event described patients choosing between affording medication or food, or how they themselves had been financially devastated by a medical crisis.

They all knew El-Sayed's rallying cry by heart, chanting it when the Michigan Democrat took the stage: "Money out of politics! Money in your pocket! Medicare for All!"

Support for Medicare for All is at its highest in at least a decade, according to a new KFF poll. The survey found two-thirds of Americans now favor expanding the government health program that largely covers seniors (about half of whom are enrolled in private plans through Medicare Advantage).

But many people don't actually know how to define Medicare for All. Traditionally, the idea has been to establish a single health insurance program, run by the federal government, that would guarantee coverage for Americans and minimize or even eliminate private insurance. How much people like the idea depends on what they're told about it, pollsters have found.

Still, at a time when fewer than half of Americans say they can afford their healthcare, Medicare for All has become a progressive shorthand for radical, systemic change.

"Too many people don't have health insurance, too many people who do have insurance can't afford medical care, and many people are terrified about the costs of being sick," said Jonathan Oberlander, a professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill who specializes in the politics of healthcare reform.

"And in an electorate that wants change, that is disenchanted with the status quo, Medicare for All is an important symbol," he said.

That's why Democrats running for Senate seats in the midterm elections in such states as Maine, Minnesota, and Florida tout their support for scrapping the current health insurance system in favor of broad Medicare coverage. But nowhere is the issue as central to a race as in Michigan, where Medicare for All has become synonymous with El-Sayed.

El-Sayed, who trained as a doctor and served as Detroit's top public health official, has campaigned on Medicare for All since his unsuccessful bid for governor in 2018. To Starks-Clay, that means he has a plan and will "stick to it," she said.

That's appealing to voters right now, said Ashley Kirzinger, director of survey methodology at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News.

"When we ask people what do they want to hear from candidates in regards to healthcare, it's a plan to bring down healthcare costs," Kirzinger said.

American Dream or Pipe Dream?

Medicare for All has been the shiny object of progressive politics in previous campaigns, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders' 2016 presidential bid and the 2020 Democratic presidential primary. Its popularity rises and falls in cycles, Oberlander said. And today, people are painfully aware their care is getting more expensive and harder to access.

In the first decade or so after the passage of the Affordable Care Act in 2010, the nation's uninsured rate was cut nearly in half. Insurance companies could no longer deny people coverage based on preexisting conditions. Since then, to cover more people, 40 states plus Washington, D.C., have expanded Medicaid, the government health program for those with low incomes or disabilities.

Now it feels as if we're moving backward, Oberlander said. "We are now, in the past two years, in an era where the Trump administration and congressional Republicans have reversed that progress."

Michigan, a battleground state that President Donald Trump won in 2024, saw some of the steepest ACA plan enrollment drops after the GOP-controlled Congress allowed enhanced tax subsidies, which helped people afford their premiums, to expire at the end of last year.

Insurance companies in Michigan hiked individual marketplace rates by an average of 20%.

And up to 355,000 Michiganders are expected to lose their Medicaid coverage in 2028 because of cuts included in Trump's signature law, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to estimates from the Urban Institute, a left-leaning think tank.

At El-Sayed's town hall in Lansing, Darleana Ash said patients at the medical diagnostics lab where she works are increasingly skipping tests because they can't afford them.

Others drive hours from rural areas because their local labs have closed or are no longer in their insurance networks. She worries about the patients who must choose between their medications and groceries some months.

"If you got somebody that's 75, 80 years old, guess what? They're going to go without the medication, because they got to eat," she said.

Packed in near the front of the crowded town hall was Cindy Lou Coolich, a boisterous retiree wearing a campaign T-shirt and cowboy hat.

She spent years working for a company that helped uninsured people enroll in coverage, until she got sick herself. A bout of sepsis nearly killed her and left her disabled.

Suddenly, she was the one enrolling in Medicaid and living on $900 a month from Social Security. She lost the 15-acre horse farm she'd owned, and then everything else, she said. "Except my car."

The saving grace, oddly, was the death of her ex-husband. Because they'd been married for more than 10 years, she could benefit from his Social Security benefits. "So now I'm doing quite well!" she laughed.

But to her, it hardly seemed like the mark of a functioning healthcare system that someone had to die for things to get better.

A universal response

Democrats aren't the only ones responding to voters' healthcare discontent. Republican Mike Rogers, a former Michigan congressman and El-Sayed's opponent, recently released a brief healthcare plan.

"I just can't think of a more important issue to the people of Michigan than healthcare and costs, the rising costs," he said. At a press conference announcing his health platform, he broadly attacked El-Sayed and Medicare for All.

"[If] the government's going to give you something, they have to take it away from someone else," Rogers said.

Under Medicare for All, millions of Michiganders with private health insurance would lose that coverage, he said.

Pointing to estimates that Medicare for All would cost some $4 trillion per year, he said, "Guess what? People pay for that."

(A recent preprint study from Yale researchers found that the cost of implementing Medicare for All, estimated at $4.2 trillion, would save about $1 trillion in healthcare spending.)

Rogers' campaign declined an interview request from KFF Health News.

Concerns about increased taxation, disruption to the current system, and reduced access to services can make Medicare for All a political liability in a close election, Oberlander said.

"It doesn't matter if the fears that they're spreading are actually accurate," he said. "Politically, what matters is if they can scare people."

But even if El-Sayed wins in November, the chances of Medicare for All replacing the current system "remain very remote in the short to medium term," Oberlander said.

Given the staunch opposition from Republicans and many moderate Democrats, not to mention the lobbying power of the healthcare industry, massively overhauling the U.S. health system won't suddenly be achievable because of a single Senate candidate.

Thomas "Jermaine" Carey knows this. A self-described activist, he attended a recent El-Sayed town hall in Detroit feeling "kind of sold out" by what he calls the "straight-ticket" Democratic Party.

Medicare for All sounds good, he said. "Do I believe it?" He shrugged.

"It's still America," he said. "You still have super PACs, the lobbyists that control everything."

This story was produced as part of NPR's health reporting collaboration with KFF Health News, a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

entries.title: 3 years on, Israelis grapple with reports Netanyahu was warned before Oct. 7 attacks
entries.summary: On the three-year mark since the Hamas-led deadly attack, Israelis are grappling with reports that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was repeatedly warned by regional allies ahead of time.
entries.content:
TEL AVIV, Israel — As Israel marks three years since Hamas launched its surprise Oct. 7 attacks, Israelis are reeling from new revelations in Israeli and U.S. media that the country had been repeatedly warned by its regional allies that Hamas was planning to attack.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was personally warned about a potential Hamas attack, and his security agencies were notified repeatedly, in the weeks and days leading up to Oct. 7, 2023, four people in the Middle East with direct knowledge of the warnings told NPR.

The Israeli newspaper Haaretz, The New York Times and The Atlantic first reported about the warnings.

Netanyahu has denied he was warned, calling the reports "fake news" and filing a defamation lawsuit last week against Israeli news outlets that published them. He and his defense minister have issued new warnings that Hamas could try to attack or "challenge" Israel on this Oct. 7 memorial day and leading up to national elections later this month.

But the Oct. 7, 2023, security failure — as well as Netanyahu's repeated refusal to take responsibility for it — has become a lightning rod in Israel as the prime minister seeks a new term in national elections this month.

"You didn't protect my son," yelled out one bereaved Israeli father whose son was killed in the Hamas-led attack, as the prime minister spoke at a memorial ceremony this week for the victims.

Middle East

Israelis grapple with reports that Netanyahu was warned of Oct. 7 attacks years ago

A message from Hamas' leader in Gaza

One warning came directly from the leader of Hamas in Gaza weeks before Oct. 7, a Palestinian mediator told NPR and other media outlets.

Former Palestinian Authority official Sufian Abu Zaida said he helped mediate secret Hamas-Israel talks for more than a year leading up to Oct. 7. He said Hamas wanted Israel to release Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and offered in exchange to release two living Israeli hostages and the bodies of two Israeli soldiers held in Gaza for years. But he said Israel was unwilling to release as many prisoners as Hamas had demanded.

On Sept. 14, 2023, Abu Zaida said, Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar dictated a message for him to deliver to Israel: "By the end of September, we will put cards on the table. There will be an earthquake in the negotiations, and the Israelis should prepare to empty their prisons."

He did not know what kind of earthquake Sinwar meant, but he said he sent the message to an Israeli intelligence official who acknowledged receiving it and to Mohammed Dahlan, a Palestinian confidant of the leader of the United Arab Emirates.

"What happened [on] the 7th of October is needless," Abu Zaida told NPR.

A telephone call from the Emirati leader

Days before the Oct. 7 attacks, the leader of the United Arab Emirates, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, called Netanyahu and told him that Hamas' leader in Gaza was planning a big assault against Israel, according to a person close to Dahlan. Dahlan was the Palestinian Authority's head of security in Gaza before Hamas seized control of the territory in 2007.

The Emirati leader told Netanyahu in a phone call that lasted more than 40 minutes that a "quake" would hit the region if no progress was achieved regarding a prisoner deal between Hamas and Israel, the person said.

The person spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity because of the diplomatic sensitivity of the call. The phone call was previously reported by Haaretz and The New York Times.

The UAE did not deny the report, saying only that it maintained dialogue with Israel.

Egypt's top intelligence chief warned Israel, an official says

A senior Egyptian official told NPR that Egypt had specific intelligence about Hamas movements and that Egypt's head of intelligence at the time, Abbas Kamel, had traveled to Israel with two other senior officials and met with Israel's Mossad and Shin Bet intelligence chiefs.

The official said Kamel relayed a warning that Gaza was on the verge of an "explosion" because of Israel's blockade, the condition of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and concerns that Israel might move to annex the occupied West Bank.

The official was not authorized to speak publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity. The Atlantic reported that Kamel's visit to Israel was on Sept 26.

A former Israeli adviser says Egypt repeatedly warned Israel

Nimrod Novik, a fellow at the Israel Policy Forum think tank and a former top adviser to late Israeli Prime Minister Shimon Peres, told NPR that he was informed before Oct. 7 by a person with firsthand knowledge that Egypt had delivered warnings to several senior Israeli officials that "Gaza is about to explode in your face."

Novik said one warning was an "urgent and dramatic message" from Egypt, delivered to a person close to Netanyahu some 10 days prior to Oct. 7.

"I'm certain that the issue of the early warnings on October 7 is going to continue to play with heightened emotions as we approach Election Day," said Novik. "This is going to be an indictment for history, not just for the elections."

Netanyahu has blamed Israeli security organizations for failing to stop the Oct. 7 attacks. He and his government have yet to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the failures around Oct. 7, despite public demand.

The new reports about warnings issued to Israel "actually turn the story on its head," pointing the finger right back at the prime minister, said Gayil Talshir, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

"It violates the basic narrative that Netanyahu tries to tell Israelis," said Talshir.

NPR's Aya Batrawy contributed to this report.

entries.title: Deep in Appalachia, a rail-to-trail project builds bipartisan support for a bridge
entries.summary: The Trump administration has been hostile to federal spending on bicycle and pedestrian infrastructure. But there's bipartisan support for a multiuse trail that would connect Ohio and West Virginia.
entries.content:
Deep in Appalachia, a rail-to-trail project builds bipartisan support for a bridge

STEUBENVILLE, Ohio — The Market Street Bridge still looms over the Ohio River, spanning almost 1,800 feet between downtown Steubenville and the green hills around Weirton, W.Va., on the other side.

But this once majestic steel suspension bridge closed nearly three years ago. And up close, it's easy to see why transportation officials consider it beyond repair.

"You got severe rusting under here," explains Michael Paprocki, a regional transportation planner, as he points to visible holes in the rusted beams under the bridge's deck. "In reality, if it stood long enough, it would probably collapse under its own weight."

Local leaders say it's crucial to replace this bridge to reconnect the communities on either side. But it's also important for another reason: The Ohio River is a major obstacle in the path of the Great American Rail-Trail, an ambitious plan to turn former rail corridors into bike and pedestrian trails that stretch from coast to coast.

Political gridlock in Washington is slowing down bicycle and pedestrian trails. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has made clear that he doesn't want to spend federal dollars on what he calls "DEI bike lanes."

But deep in Appalachia, there is bipartisan support for a multiuse trail that would connect Ohio and West Virginia. Mayors from both sides of the river — and both sides of the political divide — say the trail is vital to the region's economic future.

That's why local movers and shakers gathered a few weeks ago on the Ohio side of the bridge to talk about how to make its proposed replacement a reality.

"This is huge," said Republican Ralph Petrella, the mayor of Steubenville. In an interview with NPR, Petrella said the bridge and trail would help raise the city's profile. "This is a national entity that would help our economic development and continue the momentum we have for revitalization."

The Democratic mayor of nearby Weirton, W.Va., was on hand too. Dean Harris worked at a local steel mill for 48 years. The mill closed in 2024, and Harris says Weirton is trying to attract new employers.

"Weirton is in the process of sort of rebranding ourselves. Steel is what made us, and brought people to our area. But obviously it's time for us to move on from that," Harris said. "We need to look at the future and what's going to be good for future generations. And that's what we're in the process of doing."

Harris says the rail-trail project is part of that effort. Weirton already has a rail-trail that connects to the suburbs of Pittsburgh, about 30 miles east. That helped Weirton attract a battery factory that opened several years ago, Harris said.

Local leaders also hope the rail-trail will encourage more young people to stay. Maura Barnes grew up in Ohio near Steubenville. While most of her friends moved away, Barnes stayed after college to raise her own family in downtown Steubenville.

"My husband and I, somewhat selfishly, really wanted a grocery store in walking distance, not just for ourselves and our family, but all the other people living in the downtown community," she said.

So Barnes and her husband opened the Steubenville Grocery Box with some friends. But she says the closing of the Market Street Bridge hit the neighborhood hard.

"I think a lot of it was almost spiritual," Barnes said. "It's a loss, and it was a blow to the morale of the community."

The Veterans Memorial Bridge, less than 2 miles away, carries highway traffic over the Ohio River. But the Market Street Bridge was the only way for pedestrians or bikes to cross safely, and the only bridge that brought cars directly into downtown.

"A lot of the businesses around us who had been open for years, they saw a pretty notable decrease in foot traffic and car traffic to their businesses when that closed," Barnes said.

There is a plan to replace the Market Street Bridge with another one a few blocks away that would include a dedicated trail for bikes and pedestrians. Congress has appropriated $87 million so far. But that's only a fraction of what the new bridge will actually cost.

"The challenge of crossing a body of water as big as the Ohio River is monumental," said Eric Oberg, the senior director of programs at the Rails To Trails Conservancy, the nonprofit group behind the Great American Rail-Trail.

More than half of the proposed 3,700-mile trail already exists, Oberg said, although there are still some big gaps, including the Ohio River crossing. That's why the group organized the September event in Steubenville.

Local leaders are pushing state and federal lawmakers to find more money for the bridge. And they're focused on the surface transportation reauthorization bill that's currently being negotiated.

But they're doing it at a time when the Trump administration has been hostile to federal spending on bike infrastructure. Oberg says that creates "headwinds" for projects like this, though it doesn't have to stop progress on the replacement bridge.

"It's gonna happen. This is an inevitable project. There's too much support for it. The question is the timeline," Oberg said.

In its heyday, the Market Street Bridge used to carry 40,000 cars a year, said

Michael Paprocki, the regional transportation planner, who grew up in Steubenville. But the cables that anchor the bridge's piers to the ground have failed, leading West Virginia officials to close the bridge in late 2023.

Paprocki now serves as executive director of the Brooke Hancock Jefferson Metropolitan Planning Commission, a nonprofit working on transportation issues in the Steubenville and Weirton region. He says there's broad support for a new bridge on both sides of the political divide.

"It's not just liberals that ride bikes," he said. "Ohio is an extremely conservative state and a lot of them ride bikes. West Virginia is an extremely red state. And believe me, they love to go out and ride their bikes."

entries.title: Carpetbagger allegation, misplaced valor make Nevada's safe red House seat competitive
entries.summary: Northern Nevada has a reliably red congressional seat, represented by a Republican since it was drawn in the early 1980s. A complicated candidate and a potential blue wave this year could change that.
entries.content:
Carpetbagger allegation, misplaced valor make Nevada's safe red House seat competitive

Carpetbagger allegation, misplaced valor make Nevada's red House seat competitive

RENO, Nev. — The race for Nevada's 2nd Congressional District shouldn't be competitive, just based on history and math. But the Republican Party's nominee, David Flippo, is facing an unusually tough race despite having President Trump's endorsement, bogged down by allegations that he exaggerated his military service and lacks real ties to the district.

"This seat is some kind of competitive like it has never been in the history since it was created," said Mark Amodei, the retiring Republican congressman who has represented the northern Nevada district for the past 15 years. "And you know what I attribute that to? I attribute it to the candidate and the way he's run his campaign."

The Washington Post was first to report that Flippo's campaign repeatedly mischaracterized his military service, in fundraising appeals and a video from an earlier congressional run. In the video, the booming voice of a narrator described Flippo as "a recipient of the Bronze Star that he received for Valor."

Candidate blames young staff and grandkids

But Flippo didn't receive a bronze star with the "V" for valor, which requires bravery in battle. It's a big distinction that most veterans notice. Flippo held a press conference where he apologized and blamed a young staffer for mixing up the word "valor" from an award his whole unit received. In an interview with NPR, Flippo said the language about his awards got "edited and convoluted" and he "missed it," then caught it, but somehow it worked its way back into his campaign materials. Still, Flippo said he accepts responsibility.

"Look, part of leadership is taking ownership," he said. "It was just an honest oversight."

Flippo defended wearing the "V" on a ball cap next to his Bronze Star medal. In fact, a photo prominently displayed on his campaign website, showed him wearing two bronze "V" pins. He also wore it regularly at campaign events, including his primary night victory party. This was initially noted by the conservative outlet Nevada News & Views but Flippo addressed the question of why he was displaying those two "V" pins for the first time publicly in his interview with NPR.

"You know if you've lived with grandkids, and you know, you kind of know, when you ask them to put those things on your hat," Flippo said before offering further evidence. "Actually, answer me this. I do have another hat that's just like it, because you misplace one or whatever, and that does not have any V devices on it, so and I was like 'where did that other V device go?' So, the grandkids ended up doing that."

The campaign removed the photo from his website shortly after our interview. Flippo chalked the controversy up to politics.

"It's just crazy what people are going to go after," he said.

Brand new to the district

Earlier this year, Flippo was running for congress in Las Vegas when Amodei announced he would be retiring. So Flippo swapped districts to run for the open seat, some seven hours to the north by car from where he had been running.

With the neon Reno arch behind him and a Trump 47 hat on his head, Flippo announced in a video that he was all in for Nevada's 2nd Congressional District. The district was drawn in 1981 to be strongly Republican and Democrats have never even come close to winning here.

"This is a strong conservative district," Flippo said in an interview with NPR. "I was talking with the people that have endorsed me such as Turning Point and other organizations that are on the conservative side. The belief was that this being a conservative district we should get somebody that is more conservative in this seat."

Flippo handily won the Republican primary with Trump's endorsement. But in recent weeks Republican super PACs have had to come to Flippo's rescue with more than $1 million in TV and digital advertising reservations, according to AdImpact data.

"They must have gotten a poll and had a five alarm fire at headquarters and said we have to pour hundreds of thousands of dollars into that district to save this guy," said Jon Ralston, a longtime Nevada political journalist and founder of the Nevada Independent.

Trump won this district by 14 points two years ago, and while Ralston is skeptical a Democrat can ultimately win, he sees signs everywhere that Republicans are treating this like a real race.

Earlier this week, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added Flippo's opponent Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson to its competitive "Red to Blue" program, meaning she'll get extra support from the party committee, which sees this as a winnable race.

"In the state legislature, Teresa was known for crossing the aisle and doing what's right for Northern Nevadans," DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene said in a statement. "Against a scandal-plagued opponent who even Republicans don't like, Teresa is the leader Nevada families deserve."

At a recent candidate meet and greet in southern Reno, Benitez-Thompson played up her deep roots in the district, going back to her early childhood.

"This is home," she said, a not so subtle nod to the fact that her opponent was living and running for office in an entirely different part of the state just six months ago.

A former Miss Nevada, she's now raising four children in Reno. Something she talks about with voters a lot is affordability, including sky-high gas prices and expensive groceries.

"Look, when I talk about the fact that I'm in the middle of this with everyone I really mean it," she tells a voter. "No one has to give me talking points on the cost of groceries. I know exactly what a full grocery cart looks like. I know exactly what prices have been doing in the last year."

But there are far more Republican and independent voters in this district than Democrats, a mathematical obstacle for Benitez-Thompson.

"Literally if someone stands still for 5 seconds, I will talk to them," she said in an interview conducted in her kitchen while making her two youngest children an after school snack. "We have focused a lot on reaching outside our Democratic circle."

The candidate meet and greet was attended by voters with a wide range of political affiliations from a conservative-leaning Trump voter who asked Benitez-Thompson about socialism to a Democrat who complained she was too moderate.

Grant Sims and his daughter Jessica Sims said they don't always agree politically. He's a former Republican turned independent hoping a blue wave will send a message. She's a Democrat who ticked through a laundry list of concerns about Flippo.

"My brother was in the Marine Corps," Jessica Simms said in explaining her concerns with Flippo's Bronze Star controversy. "Even if he did receive a certain type of medal, but claiming it's more than what he received, I'm not OK with it at all. And I don't like the carpetbagging of him. You know, moving up here because there is a vacancy in the House."

A question hanging over this race, where there hasn't been any recent public polling, is whether these concerns about Flippo have broken through more broadly with voters.

The top issue is affordability

Benitez-Thompson argues that Congress needs to step up and put a check on President Trump and his policies, including the trade wars and his war with Iran, which voters blame for the high prices hitting their family budgets.

Flippo also says affordability is a problem, and admits "the cost of living is not in our favor right now."

But he strongly supports the war with Iran and like President Trump sees the elevated prices Americans are experiencing as short term pain, worth it if Iran is prevented from getting a nuclear weapon.

"I feel very confident that once this is taken care of, we'll see gas prices go right back down," he said.

Flippo's military service is a key part of his pitch to voters. In the interview with NPR, he described several tours through the middle east over a 24 year career in the Air Force, including time as a logistics commander, standing up air bases in Iraq.

"My whole career was spent eating the dust and dirt there in the Middle East and that's why I have an understanding of what's going on right now with Iran," he said.

Campaign finance records indicate he's loaned $1.6 million to his campaigns this election cycle, a significant share of his reported personal wealth. Flippo said he recently sold his businesses to prepare for serving in congress.

"Yeah, it's a lot, I'm not going to lie. But to me, this country's worth it," he said.

Flippo's campaign did not respond to requests for his financial disclosures, which are overdue.

A spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee said Democrats are "delusional" if they think this race is competitive.

But Rep. Mark Amodei disagrees. He said he's heard from a lot of Republicans who are reluctant to vote for Flippo. And he's adamant, he won't be endorsing the man who hopes to be his successor.

"It's like, I'm not hugging this," he said of Flippo. "I'm just not doing it. It's not my last move walking out the door."
